text: Mid-Year Population Estimates, England and Wales, June 2025
This spreadsheet contains a selection of the data tables published alongside the Office for National Statistics' Mid-Year Population Estimates June 2025.
Mid-Year Population Estimates, England and Wales, June 2025
The data tables in this spreadsheet were originally published at 9.30am 29 July 2026.
The next publication is scheduled for summer 2027.
The country and local authority codes are 9 digits long and are used as geography identifiers.

When comparing mid-year population datasets please be aware that while they are broadly comparable, different data sources and methods are used to create the estimates for England and Wales, Scotland, and for Northern Ireland. Differences can also occur between years. Please see the Quality and Methodology Guide (QMG) report linked below for more information.
Historic publication dates for mid-year population estimates statistics

The annual mid-year population estimates statistics roll forward the population statistics produced from decennial Censuses. The series of current population estimates is available from the tables page where this file is published.

Population estimates for England and Wales QMG
Further advice on the appropriate use of these data can be obtained by emailing pop.info@ons.gov.uk or phoning +44 (0)1329 444661 and asking to speak to a statistician.
Notes related to the data in this spreadsheet

Accuracy of estimates and rounding: estimates are presented unrounded. Unrounded estimates are published to enable and encourage further calculations and analysis. However, the estimates should not be taken to be accurate to the level of detail provided. Confidence Intervals for population estimates and the local authority, county, region and country level are provided in table MYE0 in this workbook. More information on the accuracy of the estimates is available in the Quality and Methodology Guide (QMG).
Population estimates for England and Wales QMG

Small counts: the estimates are produced using a variety of data sources and statistical models, including some statistical disclosure control methods, and small estimates should not be taken to refer to particular individuals.

Usual residence definitions: the estimated resident population of an area includes all those people who usually live there, regardless of nationality. Arriving international migrants are included in the usually resident population if they remain in the UK for at least a year. Emigrants are excluded if they remain outside the UK for at least a year. This is consistent with the United Nations definition of a long-term migrant. Armed forces stationed outside of the UK are excluded. Students are taken to be usually resident at their term time address.

Geography: where subnational level data are presented, the population estimates reflect boundaries in place as of April 2024. The term "local authority district" refers to geographical areas in the tables which are below regions and which are not counties or metropolitan counties. In England these include unitary authorities, metropolitan districts, non-metropolitan districts and London boroughs. In Wales they are known as unitary authorities, in Scotland as council districts and in Northern Ireland as local government districts. Further information can be found in the 'geography guide' worksheet.
Use of 2024 Local authorities: this spreadsheet uses boundaries for England and Wales that existed at publication, which includes the changes made in April 2023.

Revisions to mid-2022 to mid-2024 population estimates: Population estimates for mid-2022, mid-2023 and mid-2024 have been revised to account for updated international migration. The impact of revisions is discussed in the accompanying statistical bulletin and the QMG. Comprehensive data on the revisions can be found in tables MYE7 and in the Analysis of population estimates tool.
Analysis of population estimates tool for UK
Geographical coverage: these statistics cover England and Wales only. Estimates for the whole of the UK, covering mid-2025, will be published later in the year.

Uncertainty measures: The uncertainty estimates include potential uncertainty associated with the 2021 Census, international migration and internal migration. The methodology assumes all other components of population change and adjustments contain no error (e.g. births, deaths, static populations, asylum seekers, visitor switchers, boundary and reconciliation adjustments).

Confidence intervals: The unrounded confidence intervals are published to enable further analysis. However, the confidence intervals should not be taken to be accurate to the level of detail provided.

Admin Based Migration Estimates: for Admin Based Migration Estimates (ABME), the ONS is progressing with the development of methods to quantify uncertainty with the ABME process. We have developed a simulation based approach for the headline Long Term International Migration (LTIM) uncertainty from ABMEs: Measuring uncertainty in international migration estimates - Office for National Statistics (ons.gov.uk). However, the method only covers some sources of uncertainty with ABMEs (adjustments, modelling, and sampling variability). We have recognised that these uncertainty intervals are partial and likely overconfident with respect to uncertainty associated with ABMEs.
Measuring uncertainty in international migration estimates - Office for National Statistics (ons.gov.uk).

Scaling factors: In order to calculate uncertainty for internal migration, a benchmark approach is used treating the 2021 Census transitions as the gold standard and comparing these transitions to the 2021 Personal Demographic Service (PDS) transitions. There exists a time difference between the normal Census cutoff date (March 21st) and the PDS cutoff date (June 30th) so to generate the initial full years’ worth of uncertainty, a new version of the 2021 PDS transitions was created aligning with the 2021 Census transitions dates.  This comparison creates an element of error in the PDS transitions known as scaling factors. These scaling factors are then clustered based on identifying local authorities with a similar error pattern and then fitted to a generalized additive model (GAM) and resampled 1000 times. We resample the residuals from the models and use them to generate 1000 plausible PDS transition estimates for the future years of interest. Upper and lower bounds are then derived from the 1000 estimates.
Methodology for measuring uncertainty in ONS local authority mid-year population estimates: 2012 to 2016 - Office for National Statistics

Census uncertainty: we aim to incorporate census uncertainty by using the census bootstrapped estimates, rather than the census estimate for local authorities. Quality assurance found there was a discrepancy between the census bootstrapped estimates and the census point estimates, which is the starting point for the MYE components of change. Overall, we found that the census bootstrapped estimates were systematically lower than the census point estimates. The result was that over 50% of the MYEs were outside of their uncertainty intervals for YE June 2021. An upward adjustment was applied to the census bootstrapped estimates to mitigate against the discrepancy while retaining the variance from the bootstrapped estimates.

Bias-adjusted confidence intervals at local authority level: bias-adjusted confidence intervals are calculated as the mid-year estimate plus or minus 1.96 multiplied by RMSE. The RMSE is the variability of the simulated values around the MYE. This confidence interval will be symmetric about the MYE and will include a measure of uncertainty due to bias between the MYE and the simulations. Bias adjusted confidence intervals are the preferred measure of statistical uncertainty for the mid-year estimates but two other versions, empirical and centred are produced. Bias adjusted confidence intervals are often wider than the empirical and centred intervals.
Guidance on interpreting the statistical measures of uncertainty in ONS local authority mid-year population estimates

Centred confidence intervals for England and Wales: Centred empirical confidence intervals are created by moving the empirical 95% confidence intervals so that they are centred about the observed MYEs. The difference between the median of the simulated values and the observed MYE is subtracted from each of the lower and upper bounds. While the width of the confidence interval remains the same it does not account for the bias component due to the difference between the MYE and the median of the simulation. We recommend using centred confidence intervals for England and Wales
Guidance on interpreting the statistical measures of uncertainty in ONS local authority mid-year population estimates

Aiding understanding: uncertainty measures for mid-year estimates are presented to aid users in understanding the precision of mid-year estimates but are still research.  Further information is available from our Quality Information dataset.
Population estimates: quality information - Office for National Statistics
Accredited Official Statistics: these estimates are accredited official statistics as they have been assessed against the quality standards required for accredited official statistics status.

Internal migration: residential moves between different local authority districts in the UK, including those that cross the boundaries between the four UK nations: England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Internal migration figures for Northern Ireland include flows to and from the Isle of Man. This means that net internal migration at UK level will not sum to zero.

Other changes: changes to the size of armed forces stationed in the UK and other special population adjustments. At geographies higher than local authority, adjustments due to rounding may also be included. This means that other changes at local authority level may not sum to other changes at national level.
Rounding: the population density estimates and area measurements are displayed rounded to the nearest integer though calculations have been performed on the unrounded data.

Definitions: Standard Area Measurements (SAM) data used reflect the position as at January 2025 for England, Wales and Scotland. Land area measurements, excluding inland water, have been used in compiling these population density figures. Information on this is available from the ONS geography portal.

Changes: the area measurements are a definitive set derived from boundaries maintained by Ordnance Survey and Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland. The current measurements may differ from those published previously in tables, publications, or other statistical outputs, even allowing for boundary changes or changes to the physical structure of the land because of improvements to the source of the data.

These revisions allow for updated international migration estimates to be used. The impact of revisions is discussed in the accompanying Statistical bulletin, QMG and in the Analysis of population estimates tool.

These datasets build on the population estimates and components of change previously published by ONS covering the period 2011 to 2024, by adding the most recent data from the mid-2025 population estimates and incorporating population estimates for 2022, 2023 and 2024 revised to account for updated international migration. This offers a complete and consistent time series of estimates at detailed level from mid-2011 to mid-2025.

The estimated resident population of an area includes all people who usually live there, whatever their nationality. People arriving into an area from outside the UK are only included in the population estimates if their total stay or intended stay in the UK is 12 months or more. Visitors and short-term migrants (those who enter the UK for 3 to 12 months for certain purposes) are not included. The components of change provided in the file relate to the usual resident population only and will not show, for example, short-term migrants as part of the international migration flow. Similarly, people who leave the UK are only excluded from the population estimates if they remain, or intend to remain, outside the UK for 12 months or more. This is consistent with the United Nations recommended definition of an international long-term migrant. Members of UK and non-UK armed forces stationed in the UK are included in the population and UK forces stationed outside the UK are excluded. Students are taken to be resident at their term time address.

Geographical coverage: this table covers Mid-year 2021 to Mid-year 2022 population change for England and Wales.

Internal migration: residential moves between different local authority districts in the UK, including those that cross the boundaries between the four UK nations: England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Internal migration figures for Northern Ireland include flows to and from the Isle of Man. This means that net internal migration at UK level will not sum to zero.

Other changes: changes to the size of armed forces stationed in the UK and other special population adjustments. At geographies higher than local authority, adjustments due to rounding may also be included. This means that other changes at local authority level may not sum to other changes at national level.
Rounding: the population density estimates and area measurements are displayed rounded to the nearest integer though calculations have been performed on the unrounded data.

Definitions: Standard Area Measurements (SAM) data used reflect the position as at 31 December 2022 for England, Wales and Scotland. Land area measurements, excluding inland water, have been used in compiling these population density figures. Information on this is available from the ONS geography portal. For Northern Ireland SAM data consistent with that used in their 2021 census and mid-year estimate reporting has been used.

Changes: the area measurements are a definitive set derived from boundaries maintained by Ordnance Survey and Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland. The current measurements may differ from those published previously in tables, publications, or other statistical outputs, even allowing for boundary changes or changes to the physical structure of the land because of improvements to the source of the data.

These datasets contain the most detailed population estimates and components of change for the mid-year population series. These time series offer users a rich source of data from which to conduct further investigation and research. The series are updated annually as part of each mid-year estimates release.

These datasets build on the population estimates and components of change previously published by ONS covering the period 2011 to 2022, by adding the most recent data from the mid-2022 population estimates and incorporating population estimates for 2012 to 2021 revised in light of the 2021 census in England and Wales. This offers a complete and consistent time series of estimates at detailed level from mid-2011 to mid-2022.

These datasets provide the most detailed population estimates and components of change for the mid-year population series for 2011-2022 and are consistent with the results of the 2021 Census.

These unrounded estimates are published to enable and encourage further calculations and analysis. However, the estimates should not be taken to be accurate to the level of detail provided.
More information on the accuracy of the estimates is available in the Quality and Methodology document. Appropriate methods of disclosure control have been applied to prevent inference of information relating to individuals.

The estimated resident population of an area includes all people who usually live there, whatever their nationality. People arriving into an area from outside the UK are only included in the population estimates if their total stay or intended stay in the UK is 12 months or more. Visitors and short-term migrants (those who enter the UK for 3 to 12 months for certain purposes) are not included. The components of change provided in the file relate to the usual resident population only and will not show, for example, short-term migrants as part of the international migration flow. Similarly, people who leave the UK are only excluded from the population estimates if they remain, or intend to remain, outside the UK for 12 months or more. This is consistent with the United Nations recommended definition of an international long-term migrant. Members of UK and non-UK armed forces stationed in the UK are included in the population and UK forces stationed outside the UK are excluded. Students are taken to be resident at their term time address.

The data tables in this spreadsheet were originally published at 9.30am 15 July 2024. These tables replace data originally published on 23 November 2023 and incorporate update estimates of international migration for England and Wales.
Population estimates and components of population change, for mid-2023, were published on 15 July 2024.
